clinicalPearls: Extremely rare autosomal recessive acute hepatic porphyria caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in ALAD, encoding delta-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase (porphobilinogen synthase); only a handful of confirmed cases have been described worldwide.

Clinically resembles other acute hepatic porphyrias with acute neurovisceral attacks: severe abdominal pain, vomiting, peripheral motor neuropathy and, in the most severe infantile cases, respiratory failure.

Biochemical hallmark is markedly raised urinary delta-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) with normal or only mildly raised porphobilinogen (PBG) — a pattern that distinguishes it from acute intermittent porphyria, where both are grossly elevated.
Urinary and erythrocyte coproporphyrin III is characteristically increased, and the enzyme defect is confined to the final common step before porphobilinogen formation.

The identical biochemical picture (raised ALA, near-normal PBG) is seen in lead poisoning and hereditary tyrosinaemia type I, both of which inhibit the same enzyme and must be excluded before the diagnosis is accepted.

Erythrocyte ALA dehydratase activity is grossly reduced and does not correct with in-vitro addition of a reducing sulphydryl agent (dithiothreitol), whereas lead-induced inhibition is at least partly restored — a useful discriminating test.

Attacks are managed as for acute porphyria: remove precipitants, provide adequate carbohydrate, give intravenous haem preparation early, and offer supportive neurological and respiratory care; some severe childhood cases have required liver transplantation.

Confirmation requires demonstration of biallelic pathogenic ALAD variants together with the characteristic enzymatic and porphyrin-precursor profile; heterozygous carriers are asymptomatic despite roughly half-normal enzyme activity.
reference.pathophysiology: ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in ALAD, the gene encoding delta-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase (also called porphobilinogen synthase), the cytosolic zinc-dependent enzyme that condenses two molecules of delta-aminolaevulinic acid to form the monopyrrole porphobilinogen — the second step of haem biosynthesis. Loss of enzyme activity blocks this condensation, so the pathway substrate ALA accumulates while its immediate product porphobilinogen is not overproduced, giving the distinctive precursor pattern of grossly raised ALA with only modestly elevated porphobilinogen. As in the other acute hepatic porphyrias, the accumulated ALA is thought to be the principal neurotoxin, and its overproduction is amplified when hepatic haem demand rises and derepresses the rate-limiting enzyme ALA synthase; this explains the episodic, attack-based neurovisceral phenotype rather than a chronic cutaneous one. ALA dehydratase is exquisitely sensitive to inhibition by lead, which displaces the catalytic zinc, and to succinylacetone, a structural analogue of ALA that accumulates in hereditary tyrosinaemia type I; both phenocopy the disorder biochemically. Because the enzyme is functionally homotetrameric or octameric, some disease-associated alleles act by destabilising subunit assembly, and residual activity in patients is typically only a small fraction of normal, well below the roughly half-normal activity seen in unaffected heterozygous carriers.
additionalDifferentials: Acute intermittent porphyria (both ALA and porphobilinogen grossly raised)
Lead poisoning (plumbism) inhibiting the same enzyme
Hereditary tyrosinaemia type I with succinylacetone-mediated enzyme inhibition
Hereditary coproporphyria and variegate porphyria presenting with neurovisceral attacks
Guillain-Barre syndrome and other acute motor neuropathies
Acute surgical abdomen and other causes of severe unexplained abdominal pain
Styrene or other environmental toxin exposure affecting haem synthesis
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary delta-aminolaevulinic acid and porphobilinogen (fresh, protected from light)
Urinary, faecal and erythrocyte porphyrin fractionation showing raised coproporphyrin III
Erythrocyte ALA dehydratase activity assay with and without a reducing sulphydryl agent
Blood lead concentration and iron studies to exclude plumbism
Plasma and urine succinylacetone and tyrosine metabolites to exclude tyrosinaemia type I
Molecular genetic testing for biallelic ALAD variants
Nerve conduction studies and respiratory function monitoring during attacks
redFlags: Progressive limb weakness or bulbar involvement heralding respiratory muscle failure
Hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuresis during an acute attack
Severe autonomic instability with tachycardia and labile blood pressure
Neonatal or early-childhood presentation with failure to thrive and neuropathy
Rapidly rising urinary ALA with worsening neurological signs
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on severity and age at onset, ranging from severe infantile disease with recurrent life-threatening attacks to milder adolescent-onset forms; early recognition, avoidance of precipitants and prompt haem therapy improve outcomes, though some children have required liver transplantation. With attentive metabolic care many patients achieve prolonged periods free of attacks, but the disorder carries lifelong risk of acute neurovisceral crises.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the case as acute intermittent porphyria without noting that porphobilinogen is only mildly raised while ALA is grossly elevated
Failing to exclude lead poisoning and tyrosinaemia type I, which reproduce the identical biochemical pattern
Attributing symptoms to a surgical abdomen and proceeding to unnecessary laparotomy
Overlooking the diagnosis in a symptomatic child because the disorder is assumed to be exclusively adult
Prescribing porphyrinogenic drugs during an attack and worsening the neurovisceral crisis
